To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cyclic AMP (cAMP), via increased cellular levels, causes an increase in short circuit currents, a decrease in electrical conductance, and a decrease in the relative permeability of chloride to sodium in rabbit ileum.

theophyllinc, a potent inhibitor of cyclic 3,5-AMP (cAMP) phosphodiesterase, and cholerogen, which stimulates adenylate cyclase and increases intracellular levels of cAMP, reduce the electrical conductance and permsectivity of the in vitro ileal epithelium.

theophyllin and choleragen increase the electrical resistance of the in vitro ileum by reducing the magnitude of the transepithelical shunt path, and that the permselectivity of this pathway is altered by theophylline but not by choleragen.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of ion transport in rabbit ileum.
the role of cyclic 3'5' adenosine monophosphate (cyclic AMP) and its derivatives in the control of intestinal ion transport and the regulation of the transepithel1al shunt path.
the effects of cyclic AMP on intestinal transport and permeability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

theophyllin and choleragen reduce ileal conductance by decreasing the magnitude of the transepithelia1 shunt path, and that this decrease may be accompanied by a change in the permselectivity of the shunt path.
theophyllin and choleragen increase the transepitheliai resistance of the ileum by reducing both the shunt conductance and the permeability of the shunt to Cl.
theophyllinc and choleragen increase epithelial cAMP and that this change reduces the conductance of the shunt path and alters the permselectivity of this path.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
increased epithelial cAMP levels cause a reduction in transepithelial conductance by altering the magnitude and/or the permselectivity of the transepitheliul shunt pathway.
increased epithelial cAMP levels reduce the magnitude of a transepithelial pathway which is relatively more permeable to Cl than either Na or K.
theophyllinc and choleragen reduce the magnitude of transepithelial electrical shunts, and theophylline increases the relative permeability of the shunt path to Cl.

theophyllin and choleragen increase the transepithial resistance and change the relative permeabilities of the epithelium.

theophyllin and choleragen alter the magnitude and the permselectivity of the transepithelal pathway in rabbit ileum, and that these effects are probably mediated by the cAMP system.
